subject: Chemistry
central_question: How does the structure of the carbon–halogen bond control the preparation, physical properties, substitution, elimination and environmental behaviour of haloalkanes and haloarenes?
in_scope_units: Classification of mono-, di- and polyhalogen compounds and distinction among alkyl, allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides.
Common and IUPAC nomenclature, including geminal and vicinal dihalides.
Nature, polarity, bond length and bond enthalpy of the carbon–halogen bond.
Preparation of haloalkanes from alcohols, hydrocarbons and halogen exchange.
Preparation of haloarenes by electrophilic substitution and diazonium-salt reactions.
Reactions of haloalkanes: nucleophilic substitution, SN1, SN2, stereochemistry, elimination and reactions with metals.
Reactions of haloarenes and the low reactivity of aryl halides toward nucleophilic substitution.
Uses and environmental effects of dichloromethane, chloroform, iodoform, carbon tetrachloride, freons and DDT.
banned_topics: Alcohol and phenol chemistry beyond their use as precursors, which belongs to the next chapter.
Detailed aromatic diazonium chemistry beyond its use in preparing haloarenes, which belongs to Amines.
Full atmospheric photochemistry of ozone depletion beyond the chapter’s environmental account.

known_pitfalls.claim: Aryl halides undergo SN1 and SN2 reactions as readily as alkyl halides.
known_pitfalls.correction: Aryl C–X bonds have partial double-bond character and the carbon is sp²-hybridised, so ordinary SN1 and SN2 pathways are strongly disfavoured.

known_pitfalls.claim: SN2 substitution gives racemisation at a chiral carbon.
known_pitfalls.correction: SN2 attack occurs from the back side and gives inversion of configuration.

known_pitfalls.claim: SN1 substitution is a single concerted step.
known_pitfalls.correction: SN1 proceeds through slow ionisation to a carbocation followed by nucleophile attack and may give racemisation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Aqueous KOH and alcoholic KOH give the same major product.
known_pitfalls.correction: Aqueous KOH favours substitution to alcohol, whereas alcoholic KOH favours beta-elimination to an alkene.

known_pitfalls.claim: Chlorobenzene is strongly activating in electrophilic substitution.
known_pitfalls.correction: Halogen is deactivating by its −I effect but ortho/para directing through resonance donation.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 6.1 on the eight C₅H₁₁Br structural isomers.
Use NCERT Example 6.3 for monochlorination and hydrogen equivalence.
Apply NCERT Example 6.5 to distinguish KCN and AgCN products.
Use NCERT Examples 6.6–6.8 for SN1/SN2 reactivity and chirality.
Finish with NCERT Example 6.9 on the deactivating yet ortho/para-directing effect of chlorine.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter Exercises are numbered 6.1 to 6.22 and cover structures, preparations, reaction mechanisms, stereochemistry, haloarene reactivity, conversions and polyhalogen compounds.
